We pair a ZZ quantum feature map with binary {0, pi} encoding (features median thresholded before circuit input) to expose parity structure. A binary encoding ablation, RBF SVM trained on the identical {0, pi} features, separates encoding from circuit effects: at low complexity (n = 5 features), binary RBF achieves 83.4% +/- 1.7% and the quantum kernel 81.2% +/- 1.9%, showing encoding drives performance there. At high complexity (n = 11 features, 11 qubits, r = 3 ZZ repetitions), all classical methods collapse to near-random (approx. 50%), binary RBF reaches only 54.3% +/- 1.1%, and the quantum ZZ kernel achieves 66.3% +/- 3.2% (mean +/- std, 10 seeds), a +12.0 percentage-point margin over the binary ablation and approx. 7x higher kernel-target alignment (0.094 +/- 0.020 vs. 0.013 +/- 0.001). These results identify parity complexity as a concrete axis along which genuine quantum kernel advantage, not attributable to encoding alone, emerges.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that quantum kernel advantage for parity (XOR) classification emerges only at high parity complexity (n=11 features), where classical methods collapse to near-random (~50%) but the quantum ZZ kernel achieves 66.3% accuracy—a +12.0 point margin over the best classical baseline—with encoding effects ruled out via binary ablation.
AI.motivation: To identify whether quantum kernel advantage exists for parity (XOR) classification beyond what can be attributed to encoding alone, and to characterize the threshold behavior where genuine quantum advantage emerges as a function of parity complexity.
AI.method: Paired a ZZ quantum feature map with binary {0, π} encoding (features median-thresholded before circuit input) on parity classification tasks; used a binary encoding ablation (RBF SVM trained on identical {0, π} features) to separate encoding effects from circuit effects; varied parity complexity (n=5 to n=11 features) and measured accuracy and kernel-target alignment.
AI.result: At low complexity (n=5), binary RBF (83.4%) and quantum kernel (81.2%) perform similarly, showing encoding drives performance. At high complexity (n=11), all classical methods collapse to ~50%, binary RBF reaches 54.3%, while quantum ZZ kernel achieves 66.3% (+12.0 point margin) with ~7x higher kernel-target alignment (0.094 vs 0.013).
AI.conclusion: Parity complexity is a concrete axis where genuine quantum kernel advantage—not attributable to encoding alone—emerges, with a clear threshold behavior distinguishing regimes where classical and quantum methods perform similarly from those where quantum kernels uniquely succeed.

title: Eigenstate-Selective Entangled Two-Photon Absorption in Monolayer WSe$_2$
summary: We show that the Bell-state phase of a polarization-entangled photon pair controls the biexciton eigenstate distribution produced by entangled two-photon absorption (ETPA) in monolayer WSe$_2$. In a frequency-nondegenerate ladder scheme, two independent valley pathways ($K$ and $K'$) share no intermediate state, so the biphoton phase sets the relative amplitude between them. Within the valley-symmetric limit this phase factorizes from the material response, and the resulting selection rule partitions the excitation among biexciton eigenstates according to the Bell-state phase $\varphi$. The symmetric Bell state ($\varphi = 0$) selectively drives bright eigenstates, while the antisymmetric state ($\varphi = π$) drives the exchange-dark eigenstate. No classical polarization source reproduces this $\varphi$-dependent eigenstate distribution. Including valley dephasing and intervalley scattering at 4~K, the phase-scan visibility exceeds $0.97$ for broadband SPDC ($T_e \sim 100$~fs) with high source purity.

AI.tldr: The Bell-state phase of entangled photon pairs controls biexciton eigenstate distribution in monolayer WSe₂ via entangled two-photon absorption, enabling selective driving of bright vs. exchange-dark states with >0.97 visibility at 4K.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that the phase of entangled photon pairs can serve as a quantum control parameter for selecting biexciton eigenstates in 2D semiconductors, going beyond what classical light sources can achieve.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of entangled two-photon absorption (ETPA) in monolayer WSe₂ using a frequency-nondegenerate ladder scheme. Two independent valley pathways (K and K') share no intermediate state, with the biphoton phase setting the relative amplitude between them. Valley-symmetric limit allows phase factorization from material response.
AI.result: The symmetric Bell state (φ=0) selectively drives bright biexciton eigenstates, while the antisymmetric state (φ=π) drives the exchange-dark eigenstate. No classical polarization source reproduces this φ-dependent eigenstate distribution. Phase-scan visibility exceeds 0.97 for broadband SPDC at 4K.
AI.conclusion: Entangled two-photon absorption with controlled Bell-state phase enables selective exciton-biexciton quantum state preparation in monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides, with high fidelity achievable even under realistic decoherence conditions.

title: Electronic and Photonic Integration of Single Quantum Emitters in 2D Materials
summary: Single-photon sources that are bright, pure, and interference-ready are essential for quantum communication and photonic quantum information processing, but many solid-state platforms still rely on bulky optical excitation, careful alignment, and post-selection to achieve useful linewidth, stability, and brightness. Scalable quantum photonics instead requires turnkey quantum-light engines that can be triggered on demand, stabilized against environmental noise, and efficiently interfaced with fibers or photonic circuits. This review surveys recent progress in electronic and photonic integration of single quantum emitters in two-dimensional materials, focusing on localized excitonic emitters in transition metal dichalcogenides and defect-based color centers in hexagonal boron nitride. On the electronic side, we discuss electrical injection, fast modulation, electrostatic stabilization, and Stark tunability as routes to suppress blinking, spectral wandering, and charge-noise-induced broadening. On the photonic side, we review waveguide and resonator platforms that funnel emission into well-defined optical modes and, in some cases, enhance radiative rates through the Purcell effect. We connect these integration strategies to key source metrics, including single-photon purity, brightness, spectral stability, and photon indistinguishability. We conclude that the next stage of progress will depend on co-designed electronic and photonic architectures that jointly optimize on-demand operation, stabilization, tunability, and packaging-compatible optical interfacing.

AI.tldr: This review examines recent progress in electronic and photonic integration of single-photon emitters in 2D materials (TMDs and hBN), covering electrical control, cavity coupling, and their impact on source performance metrics, concluding that co-designed electronic-photonic architectures are needed for practical quantum photonics.
AI.motivation: Single-photon sources based on solid-state platforms still rely on bulky optics, careful alignment, and post-selection, which are not scalable. There is a need for turnkey quantum-light engines that are on-demand, stable, and efficiently interfaced with fibers or photonic circuits for quantum communication and photonic quantum information processing.
AI.method: The paper is a review that surveys electronic integration (electrical injection, fast modulation, electrostatic stabilization, Stark tuning to suppress blinking and spectral diffusion) and photonic integration (waveguides, resonators, Purcell enhancement) of single quantum emitters in 2D materials, specifically localized excitonic emitters in TMDs and defect-based color centers in hBN.
AI.result: Electronic integration enables suppression of blinking, spectral wandering, and charge-noise-induced broadening. Photonic integration funnels emission into well-defined optical modes and can enhance radiative rates via the Purcell effect. These strategies are connected to key source metrics: single-photon purity, brightness, spectral stability, and photon indistinguishability.
AI.conclusion: The next stage of progress will depend on co-designed electronic and photonic architectures that jointly optimize on-demand operation, stabilization, tunability, and packaging-compatible optical interfacing.

title: Weighted Phase-Space Paths for Exact Wigner Dynamics
summary: A quantum state can be written in phase space, but the resulting object is not generally the probability density of a positive stochastic process on ordinary phase space. We spell this out for Wigner dynamics. If a positive phase-space process is required only to reproduce the Born density after integrating over momentum, the requirement fixes only an integrated current; the local drift and diffusion remain underdetermined. If one instead requires all Weyl-ordered expectation values, the phase-space object is fixed to be the Wigner function. For non-quadratic potentials the Wigner--Moyal generator contains higher-order, signed momentum-transfer terms, so it is not the Fokker--Planck generator of a positive Brownian diffusion. The exact Wigner function must therefore be reconstructed, in a stochastic representation, as a weighted empirical measure \[ \FW(\z,t)=\E_{\Pp}[W_tδ(\z-\z_t)], \qquad \z=(q,p), \] rather than the unweighted density of sampled carrier trajectories. With classical Hamiltonian flow as the carrier, all nonclassical correction beyond classical transport sits in the Moyal residual and can be represented by signed weights or branching events. The same split defines a residual diagnostic that vanishes for quadratic Hamiltonians and measures what classical carrier transport misses in anharmonic dynamics. The formulation also gives a forward--reverse relation for signed Wigner path measures. The ratio of forward and reversed contributions separates into a positive magnitude factor and a sign factor. This sign records the parity of the Wigner interference contribution; it is not a thermodynamic entropy production.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes Wigner dynamics in phase space, showing that the Wigner function is not generally a positive stochastic probability density. It derives a stochastic representation using weighted empirical measures with signed weights, introduces a residual diagnostic for non-quadratic Hamiltonians, and clarifies that the sign factor in forward-reverse ratios records Wigner interference parity rather than thermodynamic entropy production.
AI.motivation: To clarify the stochastic interpretation of quantum Wigner dynamics in phase space, addressing the fact that the Wigner function is not generally a positive probability density, and to develop a proper stochastic representation and diagnostic tools for nonclassical corrections.
AI.method: The authors analyze Wigner-Moyal dynamics, compare conditions for positive phase-space processes vs. the exact Wigner function, derive a stochastic representation as a weighted empirical measure with signed weights or branching events, and formulate a forward-reverse relation for signed Wigner path measures.
AI.result: The Wigner function must be reconstructed as a weighted empirical measure rather than an unweighted density. A residual diagnostic is introduced that vanishes for quadratic Hamiltonians and measures what classical carrier transport misses in anharmonic dynamics. The forward-reverse ratio separates into a positive magnitude factor and a sign factor recording Wigner interference parity.
AI.conclusion: Nonclassical corrections beyond classical transport reside in the Moyal residual and can be represented by signed weights or branching events. The sign factor in forward-reverse measures is not thermodynamic entropy production but rather the parity of Wigner interference contribution.

title: Optical Pulling Force in Carbon Nanotubes: Manifestation of Nonlocal Conductivity
summary: We develop a new theory of an optical force exerted on a carbon nanotube (CNT) with a nonlocal conductivity. The optical force is expressed in terms of the surface current density and the axial electric field on the CNT surface. To determine these quantities, we employ an integral-equation-based approach in terms of the current density. The analysis is constructed for a finite-length cylindrical CNT by rigorously accounting for edge effects. In addition to numerical solutions of the integral equation, we obtain an approximate analytical expression for the optical force acting on the CNT, which shows good agreement with numerical simulations. We also demonstrate the existence of some frequency ranges in which the optical force becomes negative, corresponding to the optical pulling effect. Such a pulling behavior is shown to originate from the nonlocality of the conductivity and to vanish in the local limit. This work advances theoretical understanding of optomechanical interactions in finite-length low-dimensional conductors and clarifies the role of spatial dispersion in the emergence of optical pulling forces.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a theory of optical force on finite-length carbon nanotubes with nonlocal conductivity, demonstrating that nonlocality enables negative (pulling) optical forces, which vanish in the local limit.
AI.motivation: To advance theoretical understanding of optomechanical interactions in finite-length low-dimensional conductors and clarify the role of spatial dispersion in optical pulling forces.
AI.method: The optical force is expressed via surface current density and axial electric field on the CNT surface. An integral-equation-based approach in terms of current density is employed, rigorously accounting for edge effects. Both numerical solutions and approximate analytical expressions are derived.
AI.result: The approximate analytical expression for optical force agrees well with numerical simulations. Certain frequency ranges exhibit negative optical force (pulling effect), which originates from conductivity nonlocality and vanishes in the local limit.
AI.conclusion: Nonlocal conductivity is essential for generating optical pulling forces in finite-length carbon nanotubes, and this work advances the theory of optomechanics in low-dimensional conductors.

title: Pontus-Mpemba effect in cavity quantum electrodynamics
comment: 17 pages, 7 figures, accepted for publication in Physica A (special issue Mpemba Effect: An Anomalous Relaxation Phenomenon)
summary: The quantum Pontus-Mpemba effect is a counterintuitive phenomenon in which a quantum system relaxes faster through a two-step evolution protocol than through a single, unquenched relaxation. This work proposes its realization in cavity quantum electrodynamics using the Jaynes-Cummings model with photon loss. The model captures the coherent interaction between a two-level atom and a single quantized mode of a lossy cavity, providing a minimal yet realistic setting to explore dissipative quantum dynamics. Restricting the analysis to the single-excitation sector, the dynamics feature damped vacuum Rabi oscillations for weak dissipation that transition to near-exponential atomic decay under strong dissipation. A sudden quench of the cavity decay rate generates distinct relaxation trajectories from the same initial atom-cavity state. The atomic excitation then displays a non-monotonic, accelerated decay, where a trajectory with a quenched dissipation relaxes faster than fixed-loss evolution. The effect originates from the interplay between coherent atom-photon exchange and cavity dissipation, establishing a clear and experimentally accessible realization of the quantum Pontus-Mpemba effect in both optical and circuit QED platforms.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a realization of the quantum Pontus-Mpemba effect in cavity QED using the Jaynes-Cummings model with photon loss, where a system with a sudden quench of cavity decay rate relaxes faster than fixed-loss evolution.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that the quantum Pontus-Mpemba effect—where a quantum system relaxes faster through a two-step evolution protocol than through a single, unquenched relaxation—can be realized in a minimal, experimentally accessible cavity QED setting.
AI.method: The Jaynes-Cummings model with photon loss is analyzed in the single-excitation sector, considering damped vacuum Rabi oscillations under weak dissipation and near-exponential atomic decay under strong dissipation. A sudden quench of the cavity decay rate is applied to generate distinct relaxation trajectories from the same initial state.
AI.result: The atomic excitation displays non-monotonic, accelerated decay when a dissipation quench is applied; a trajectory with a quenched dissipation relaxes faster than the fixed-loss evolution, confirming the quantum Pontus-Mpemba effect.
AI.conclusion: The effect originates from the interplay between coherent atom-photon exchange and cavity dissipation, and it is experimentally accessible in both optical and circuit QED platforms.

title: Three wave mixing vacuum squeezing generation in a SNAIL-based Traveling-Wave Parametric Amplifier with alternated flux polarity
summary: Recent demonstrations of squeezing generation using Traveling Wave Parametric Amplifiers (TWPAs) have opened the way for the application of broadband microwave squeezing in quantum sensing, quantum-enhanced detection, and continuous-variable quantum information. Here we demonstrate vacuum squeezing generation via residual three-wave mixing (3WM) in a Josephson TWPA based on superconducting nonlinear asymmetric inductive elements (SNAILs) with alternated magnetic flux polarity. By investigating competition between four-wave mixing (4WM) and 3WM nonlinearities, we prove that vacuum squeezing generation via residual 3WM is possible when a careful choice of the operating flux point is adopted. Our study provides valuable insights on the impact of competing nonlinearities on TWPA squeezers, potentially extending the range of applications in the framework of microwave photonics.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates vacuum squeezing generation using residual three-wave mixing in a Josephson TWPA based on SNAILs with alternated magnetic flux polarity, showing that careful flux point selection enables squeezing despite competition with four-wave mixing nonlinearities.
AI.motivation: To enable broadband microwave squeezing for applications in quantum sensing, quantum-enhanced detection, and continuous-variable quantum information by leveraging traveling wave parametric amplifiers.
AI.method: Utilizing a Josephson TWPA based on SNAILs with alternated magnetic flux polarity, investigating the competition between four-wave mixing (4WM) and three-wave mixing (3WM) nonlinearities, and selecting an optimal operating flux point to enable residual 3WM squeezing.
AI.result: Vacuum squeezing generation via residual 3WM is achievable when a careful choice of the operating flux point is adopted, despite competing 4WM nonlinearities.
AI.conclusion: Provides insights on the impact of competing nonlinearities on TWPA squeezers, potentially extending applications in microwave photonics.

title: Non-Abelian String-Breaking Dynamics on a Qudit Quantum Computer
summary: Gauge theories form the foundation of the Standard Model of particle physics. These theories can exhibit confinement, where charged particles only occur in bound states, connected by flux strings whose energy grows linearly with separation. Simulating the real-time dynamics of such strings, including their breaking, remains a major challenge for classical computations and a promising target for quantum simulations. While recent quantum simulation experiments explored string-breaking dynamics in abelian lattice gauge theories, non-abelian theories are qualitatively distinct because gauge fields themselves carry charge. Here, we report the first quantum simulation of genuine non-abelian string-breaking dynamics in a pure SU($2$) lattice gauge theory, where gauge-field self-interactions drive string breaking even in the absence of dynamical matter. Our results are obtained on a trapped-ion quantum computer, using native qudit Hilbert spaces to encode truncated gauge fields on a ladder geometry and implement digital Trotter dynamics. We experimentally study unbreakable and breakable strings generated by fundamental and adjoint static charges, respectively. We locally resolve string oscillations and coherent string breaking through the creation of gluonic excitations driven by non-abelian plaquette interactions. Our work establishes hardware-efficient, problem-tailored qudit simulations as a promising route for accessing non-perturbative dynamics relevant to high-energy physics.

AI.tldr: First quantum simulation of non-abelian string-breaking dynamics in pure SU(2) lattice gauge theory using trapped-ion qudit quantum computer, demonstrating string breaking via gauge-field self-interactions without dynamical matter.
AI.motivation: Simulating real-time dynamics of flux strings and their breaking in non-abelian gauge theories is classically intractable but crucial for understanding confinement in the Standard Model; non-abelian theories are qualitatively distinct from abelian ones because gauge fields carry charge.
AI.method: Implemented on a trapped-ion quantum computer using native qudit Hilbert spaces to encode truncated gauge fields on a ladder geometry, with digital Trotter dynamics for pure SU(2) lattice gauge theory.
AI.result: Observed unbreakable strings from fundamental charges and breakable strings from adjoint charges; locally resolved string oscillations and coherent string breaking via creation of gluonic excitations driven by non-abelian plaquette interactions.
AI.conclusion: Hardware-efficient, problem-tailored qudit simulations offer a promising route for accessing non-perturbative dynamics relevant to high-energy physics.

title: Surface-Code Thresholds and Qubit Footprints in Shuttling-Based Spin-Qubit Railways
summary: We present a fault-tolerant mapping of rotated surface codes onto a $2\times N$ silicon spin-qubit railway architecture, utilizing electron shuttling to resolve the wiring fan-out bottleneck. Employing circuit-level noise modeling, we evaluate threshold performances across various noise biases. We demonstrate that shuttling check qubits instead of data qubits fundamentally improves system thresholds. Crucially, under a noise model biased towards dephasing for spin-qubit shuttling, the non-CSS XZZX surface code outperforms standard CSS variants. By tailoring the topological code to this specific inherent bias, we show that the Megaquop footprint is achievable with a distance 7 code requiring a $p = 10^{-3}$ physical error rate, highlighting a pathway for substantial hardware reductions in early fault-tolerant quantum processors.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a fault-tolerant mapping of rotated surface codes onto a 2×N silicon spin-qubit railway architecture using electron shuttling. It shows that shuttling check qubits improves thresholds, and under dephasing-biased noise, the XZZX surface code outperforms CSS variants, achieving Megaquop footprint with distance-7 code at p=10⁻³ error rate.
AI.motivation: To resolve the wiring fan-out bottleneck in silicon spin-qubit quantum processors and enable fault-tolerant quantum computing with reduced hardware overhead.
AI.method: A fault-tolerant mapping of rotated surface codes onto a 2×N silicon spin-qubit railway architecture using electron shuttling, with circuit-level noise modeling to evaluate threshold performances across various noise biases.
AI.result: Shuttling check qubits instead of data qubits fundamentally improves system thresholds. Under dephasing-biased noise for spin-qubit shuttling, the non-CSS XZZX surface code outperforms standard CSS variants. A distance-7 code at p=10⁻³ physical error rate achieves the Megaquop footprint.
AI.conclusion: By tailoring the topological code to the specific inherent bias of spin-qubit shuttling, substantial hardware reductions in early fault-tolerant quantum processors are achievable.

title: Quantum-enhanced Large Language Models on Quantum Hardware via Cayley Unitary Adapters
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have transformed artificial intelligence, yet classical architectures impose a fundamental constraint: every trainable parameter demands classical memory that scales unfavourably with model size. Quantum computing offers a qualitatively different pathway, but practical demonstrations on real hardware have remained elusive for models of practical relevance. Here we show that Cayley-parameterised unitary adapters -- quantum circuit blocks inserted into the frozen projection layers of pre-trained LLMs and executed on a 156-qubit IBM Quantum System Two superconducting processor -- improve the perplexity of Llama 3.1 8B, an 8-billion-parameter model in widespread use, by 1.4% with only 6,000 additional parameters and end-to-end inference validated on real Quantum Processing Unit (QPU). A systematic study on SmolLM2 (135M parameters), chosen for its tractability, reveals monotonically improving perplexity with unitary block dimension, 83% recovery of compression-induced degradation, and correct answers to questions that both classical baselines fail -- with a sharp noise-expressivity phase transition identifying the concrete path to quantum utility at larger qubit scales.

AI.tldr: The authors demonstrate that small quantum circuit adapters (Cayley-parameterized unitary blocks) inserted into frozen LLMs and executed on real 156-qubit IBM quantum hardware improve perplexity of Llama 3.1 8B by 1.4% using only 6,000 additional parameters, with systematic evidence of noise-expressivity phase transitions and recovery of compression-induced degradation.
AI.motivation: Classical LLM architectures require memory scaling linearly with parameter count, posing a fundamental scalability bottleneck. Quantum computing offers an alternative paradigm, but practical demonstrations of quantum-enhanced language models on real hardware for practically relevant models have not been achieved until this work.
AI.method: Cayley-parameterized unitary adapters are designed as quantum circuit blocks inserted into frozen projection layers of pre-trained LLMs. These adapters are executed on a 156-qubit IBM Quantum System Two superconducting processor. The approach is validated on Llama 3.1 8B (8B parameters) and systematically studied on SmolLM2 (135M parameters) with varying unitary block dimensions.
AI.result: Llama 3.1 8B perplexity improved by 1.4% with only 6,000 additional parameters on real QPU. For SmolLM2: monotonically improving perplexity with unitary block dimension, 83% recovery of compression-induced degradation, and correct answers to questions that classical baselines fail. A sharp noise-expressivity phase transition was identified, pointing to concrete quantum utility at larger qubit scales.
AI.conclusion: Quantum circuit adapters on real superconducting hardware can provide measurable improvements to large-scale LLMs with minimal additional parameters, and the observed phase transition suggests a viable path toward practical quantum advantage in language modeling as qubit counts increase.

title: Architecture Shape Governs QNN Trainability: Jacobian Null Space Growth and Parameter Efficiency
summary: Variational quantum circuits with angle encoding implement truncated Fourier series, and architectures arranging $N$ qubits with $L$ encoding layers each -- sharing encoding budget $E = NL$ -- generate identical frequency spectra, identical frequency redundancy, and require the same minimum parameter count for coefficient control. Despite this equivalence, trainability varies substantially with architecture shape $(N,L)$ at fixed $E$. We identify structural rank deficiency of the coefficient matching Jacobian $J$ as the mechanism responsible. For serial single-qubit architectures, we prove $\mathrm{rank}(J) \leq 2L+1$ regardless of parameter count $P$, with $\dim(\ker J) \geq P-(2L+1)$ growing without bound -- a phenomenon we term \emph{structural gradient starvation}: a growing fraction of parameters become structurally decoupled from the loss as $P$ increases at fixed $L$. Parallel architectures avoid this via independent phase trajectories, ensuring $σ_{\min}(J^{(\mathrm{par})}) > 0$ generically for $P \leq 2E+1$, so no parameter lies in $\ker J$. For practitioners, we further show that the two natural routes to increasing parameter count have fundamentally different effects: adding feature map (FM) layers monotonically strengthens the Jacobian QFIM eigenvalue spectrum and achieves $R^2 \geq 0.95$ with $1.6$--$2.2\times$ fewer parameters than adding trainable blocks across all tested architectures, while trainable blocks improve training only through the classical interpolation mechanism with no quantum-specific benefit.

AI.tldr: Variational quantum circuits with angle encoding and fixed encoding budget E=NL show equivalent frequency properties regardless of architecture shape (N,L), but trainability differs due to structural rank deficiency in the Jacobian. Serial architectures suffer from "structural gradient starvation" with rank(J) ≤ 2L+1, while parallel architectures avoid this. Adding feature map layers outperforms adding trainable blocks for improving trainability.
AI.motivation: To understand why different architectures of variational quantum circuits with identical encoding budgets exhibit substantially different trainability, despite having equivalent frequency spectra, redundancy, and parameter requirements.
AI.method: The paper identifies structural rank deficiency of the coefficient matching Jacobian J as the mechanism for trainability differences. It proves theoretical bounds on rank(J) for serial single-qubit architectures and analyzes parallel architectures. It compares two routes to increasing parameter count: adding feature map (FM) layers vs. adding trainable blocks.
AI.result: For serial architectures, rank(J) ≤ 2L+1 regardless of parameter count P, with dim(ker J) ≥ P-(2L+1) growing unboundedly ("structural gradient starvation"). Parallel architectures ensure σ_min(J^(par)) > 0 for P ≤ 2E+1. Adding FM layers strengthens the Jacobian QFIM spectrum and achieves R² ≥ 0.95 with 1.6-2.2× fewer parameters than adding trainable blocks.
AI.conclusion: Architecture shape at fixed encoding budget significantly impacts trainability. Serial architectures suffer from structural gradient starvation where more parameters become decoupled from the loss. Parallel architectures avoid this. Adding feature map layers is a more effective strategy than adding trainable blocks for improving performance.

title: Passive Imaging with Quantum Advantage
summary: Far-field optical imaging inevitably involves low-pass spatial filtering, limiting the resolution. Moreover, conventional imaging suppresses high spatial frequency components close to the cutoff, making them invisible under noise, particularly the shot noise arising from discrete and random nature of quantum light. Here we propose and implement a method for reducing the effect of this noise by optically pre-processing the incoming light prior to detection, thereby optimizing the quantum measurement performed on it. Our scheme, termed Fourier Domain Division (FDD), partitions the Fourier plane into multiple regions for independent detection and subsequent post-processing for image reconstruction. By analyzing the quantum and classical Fisher information, we show that our method is advantageous with respect to direct imaging for high spatial-frequency components. As a result, the number of photons required to achieve a certain signal-to-noise-ratio in the Fourier domain is reduced, thus enhancing the overall resolution in the photon-starved regime. We demonstrate our method in microscopy, achieving 5-fold improvement of Fisher information on high spatial-frequency components. Unlike active super-resolution methods, FDD is passive, making it broadly applicable in microscopy and other imaging scenarios where active illumination is impractical, including astronomy and remote sensing. Our work establishes a general strategy for designing quantum optimized superresolution imaging systems, bridging fundamental quantum limits, practical image analysis and computer vision applications.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Fourier Domain Division (FDD), a passive optical preprocessing method that partitions the Fourier plane for independent detection, reducing shot noise effects and enhancing resolution in photon-starved imaging regimes. It achieves a 5-fold improvement in Fisher information on high spatial-frequency components and is applicable to microscopy, astronomy, and remote sensing.
AI.motivation: Far-field optical imaging suffers from low-pass spatial filtering that limits resolution, and conventional imaging suppresses high spatial-frequency components near the cutoff, making them invisible under shot noise from quantum light. There is a need to reduce this noise effect to enhance resolution, especially in photon-starved regimes where active super-resolution methods are impractical.
AI.method: The method, Fourier Domain Division (FDD), optically pre-processes incoming light prior to detection by partitioning the Fourier plane into multiple regions for independent detection, followed by post-processing for image reconstruction. The approach is analyzed using quantum and classical Fisher information to optimize the quantum measurement.
AI.result: FDD is advantageous over direct imaging for high spatial-frequency components, reducing the number of photons required to achieve a certain SNR in the Fourier domain. A 5-fold improvement in Fisher information on high spatial-frequency components was demonstrated in microscopy.
AI.conclusion: FDD establishes a general strategy for designing quantum-optimized super-resolution imaging systems that bridge fundamental quantum limits, practical image analysis, and computer vision. It is passive and broadly applicable to microscopy, astronomy, and remote sensing where active illumination is impractical.

title: Syndrome resampling enhances quantum error correction thresholds
summary: Quantum error correction (QEC) enables fault-tolerant quantum computation but requires operating quantum hardware at physical error rates below code-dependent thresholds, which remains challenging for current devices. We introduce syndrome resampling, a general method that increases QEC thresholds of any decoder and suppresses logical errors without additional hardware, decoding modifications, or code-specific assumptions beyond syndrome statistics. The method exploits the fact that syndromes with low probability are likely to lead to logical failure, therefore biasing syndrome averages towards most likely syndromes effectively increases logical fidelities. We establish a direct connection between the Rényi coherent information (RCI) and powers of the syndrome probability distribution, showing that resampling syndromes according to these powers combined with maximum likelihood decoding (MLD) realizes a family of optimal thresholds associated with phase transitions in the RCI. Numerical simulations of surface codes demonstrate that syndrome resampling substantially increases thresholds for both optimal and suboptimal decoders and reduces logical error rates by up to four orders of magnitude in experimentally relevant regimes. We further show that syndrome resampling can be effectively implemented from finite data and combined with decoding-based post-selection to achieve additional gains. Finally, applying the method to existing experimental QEC data yields up to two orders of magnitude reduction in logical error rates without requiring additional measurements. Our results provide a practical and decoder-agnostic route to improved logical fidelities in near-term QEC experiments.

AI.tldr: Syndrome resampling is a general, hardware-free method that boosts QEC thresholds and suppresses logical errors by biasing syndrome averages toward more likely syndromes, demonstrated with up to four orders of magnitude error reduction in surface code simulations and two orders on experimental data.
AI.motivation: Current quantum hardware operates at physical error rates above code-dependent thresholds needed for fault-tolerant computation, motivating the need for methods that improve logical fidelity without requiring additional hardware or modifications to existing decoders or code-specific assumptions.
AI.method: The method exploits low-probability syndromes being linked to logical failure, so resampling syndromes according to powers of their probability distribution (connected to Rényi coherent information) biases averages toward high-likelihood syndromes, effectively increasing logical fidelities when combined with maximum likelihood decoding.
AI.result: Surface code simulations show syndrome resampling substantially increases thresholds for both optimal and suboptimal decoders, reduces logical error rates by up to four orders of magnitude, and applied to existing experimental QEC data yields up to two orders of magnitude reduction without extra measurements.
AI.conclusion: Syndrome resampling provides a practical, decoder-agnostic route to improved logical fidelities in near-term QEC experiments, with effective implementation possible from finite data and combinable with post-selection for additional gains.

title: Variationally Compressing Quantum Circuits to Approximate Nonadiabatic Molecular Quantum Dynamics
summary: Quantum simulation has begun to penetrate the field of quantum chemistry in hopes of efficiently calculating ground state energies and approximating real-time evolution. With modern research highlighting nonadiabatic dynamics, tunably approximating deep circuits representing potential landscapes becomes crucial for simulating real quantum systems. Variationally approximating unitaries allows for shallower circuits and accuracy tunable to hardware fidelity, so long as the observable quantities are preserved. We show the variational compression of Trotter terms preserve reaction rate coefficients via classical emulation of a hybrid quantum-classical optimization method, as well as fast-forwarded adiabatic dynamics on quantum hardware. Compressed circuits can be incorporated with product-formula-based time evolution to approximate dynamics of a particle in two coupled harmonic potentials, allowing tunability when removing high-cost qubit interactions. Approximate rate coefficients are recovered after substituting terms in a nonadiabatic dynamic process, giving proof-of-principle for observable preservation under variational optimization. Attention is paid to minimizing qubit and gate-count resources.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that variational compression of Trotter terms preserves reaction rate coefficients in nonadiabatic quantum dynamics, enabling shallower, hardware-tunable circuits for simulating quantum chemical systems like a particle in coupled harmonic potentials.
AI.motivation: Nonadiabatic dynamics in quantum chemistry require deep circuits to represent complex potential landscapes; variational approximation of unitaries can produce shallower, fidelity-tunable circuits if observable quantities are preserved.
AI.method: Classical emulation of a hybrid quantum-classical optimization method for variational compression of Trotter terms, combined with fast-forwarded adiabatic dynamics on quantum hardware. Compressed circuits are incorporated with product-formula-based time evolution.
AI.result: Approximate reaction rate coefficients are recovered after substituting terms in a nonadiabatic dynamic process, demonstrating observable preservation under variational optimization. Resources (qubits and gate count) are minimized.
AI.conclusion: Variational compression preserves key observables (reaction rate coefficients) in nonadiabatic dynamics, providing proof-of-principle for using shallower, tunable circuits in quantum chemistry simulations on near-term hardware.

title: Matrix encoding method in variational algorithm of calculating eigenvalues and generalized eigenvalues
summary:
We propose a variational method for constructing the eigenvalues and generalized eigenvalues for an arbitrary $N\times N$ complex matrix. The quantum part of our algorithm is based on encoding the matrix elements into the pure state of a quantum system and expressing the loss function with optimization parameters in terms of certain probability amplitudes in the superposition state. The principal step of this algorithm is the measurement of the ancilla state
  that removes all extra terms from the above superposition and allows to probabilistically construct the required loss function along with its derivatives with respect to the optimization parameters. These output data are used to find the new values of optimization parameters for the next iteration of the loss function in the gradient optimization method. The depth and size of the circuit for this algorithm are, respectively, $O(N^2 \log N)$ and $O(\log N)$.

AI.tldr: A variational quantum algorithm for computing eigenvalues and generalized eigenvalues of arbitrary N×N complex matrices, using a circuit with O(N² log N) depth and O(log N) size.
AI.motivation: To develop a quantum algorithm capable of handling arbitrary (non-Hermitian) complex matrices for eigenvalue problems, which are computationally expensive classically.
AI.method: Matrix elements are encoded into a pure quantum state; a loss function is expressed in terms of probability amplitudes; ancilla measurement removes extra superposition terms to construct the loss function and its gradients; gradient optimization iteratively updates parameters.
AI.result: The algorithm achieves circuit depth O(N² log N) and circuit size O(log N).
AI.conclusion: The proposed variational method provides a probabilistic quantum approach to eigenvalue and generalized eigenvalue problems for arbitrary complex matrices with favorable circuit complexity.

title: Universal Analog Quantum Simulation
summary: Analog quantum simulators emulate complex many-body dynamics through native continuous-time evolution under hardware-defined interactions. Yet once a platform is specified, its interaction structure is largely fixed by the underlying hardware, restricting the Hamiltonians that can be realized and limiting programmability. Here we introduce universal analog quantum simulation (UAQS), a hybrid framework that systematically expands the range of accessible quantum evolutions within a given analog platform. UAQS employs optimized continuous-time control fields to engineer target dynamics directly, avoiding decomposition into discrete gate sequences. By preserving native analog evolution while extending the set of achievable Hamiltonians, UAQS transforms fixed-interaction analog devices into programmable simulators. Numerical studies on representative architectures, including superconducting circuits and Rydberg-atom arrays, show that UAQS accurately reproduces non-trivial many-body dynamics beyond the intrinsic interaction structure of the hardware. These results establish UAQS as a practical route toward programmable analog quantum simulation.

AI.tldr: UAQS is a hybrid framework that uses optimized continuous-time control fields to expand the range of Hamiltonians realizable on fixed-interaction analog quantum simulators, enabling programmable simulation without discrete gate decomposition.
AI.motivation: Analog quantum simulators have fixed interaction structures determined by hardware, which restricts the Hamiltonians they can realize and limits programmability.
AI.method: UAQS employs optimized continuous-time control fields to engineer target dynamics directly within native analog evolution, avoiding decomposition into discrete gate sequences.
AI.result: Numerical studies on superconducting circuits and Rydberg-atom arrays show UAQS accurately reproduces non-trivial many-body dynamics beyond the hardware's intrinsic interaction structure.
AI.conclusion: UAQS provides a practical route toward programmable analog quantum simulation by transforming fixed-interaction analog devices into flexible simulators.

title: Finite-size general security for differential phase shift keying via variable-length quantum key distribution
summary: Differential phase shift keying (DPSK) constitutes a pathway towards practical quantum key distribution by using affordable commercial technologies, and robust theoretical foundations. Recent advances in the security of DPSK have proven its security against general adversaries, albeit requiring limitations, including strong repetition rate constraints at the security proof and costly statistical estimators. In this work, we overcome said limitations by leveraging recent techniques in variable-length general security by using entropy accumulation techniques based on Rényi leftover hashing, together with conic optimization methods. Our approach achieves secret key rates with $10^5$ signals beyond 12 dB, constituting a robust proof of the experimental implementability of industrial-grade DPSK.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a new security proof for DPSK QKD that overcomes repetition rate constraints and costly statistical estimators by combining variable-length general security, entropy accumulation via Rényi leftover hashing, and conic optimization, achieving secret key rates exceeding 12 dB with 10^5 signals, demonstrating industrial-grade implementability.
AI.motivation: Previous DPSK security proofs required strong repetition rate constraints and costly statistical estimators, limiting practical implementation despite DPSK's promise for affordable commercial QKD. The authors aim to overcome these limitations to enable industrial-grade DPSK.
AI.method: The authors leverage variable-length general security techniques, entropy accumulation based on Rényi leftover hashing, and conic optimization methods.
AI.result: Achieves secret key rates with 10^5 signals beyond 12 dB, proving experimental implementability of industrial-grade DPSK.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach constitutes a robust proof that DPSK can be practically implemented with industrial-grade components, removing prior restrictions on repetition rates and statistical estimators.

title: Meromorphic Quantum Computing
summary: We consider the kinematic axioms of quantum mechanics projectively. Instead of normalized (pure) states up to global phase, states become one-dimensional subspaces of vector spaces. This process of projectivization is functorial and lax monoidal. For qubits it identifies the Bloch sphere with the Riemann sphere. We interpret a fragment of the ZXW-calculus projectively and thereby provide an alternate derivation of the arithmetic GHZ/W-calculus of Coecke et al. We find meromorphic functions that characterize the coherent behaviour of circuits for logical state preparation of quantum codes and magic state distillation.

AI.tldr: The paper projectivizes quantum mechanical kinematic axioms, making states one-dimensional subspaces rather than normalized vectors up to global phase. This functorial, lax monoidal process identifies the qubit Bloch sphere with the Riemann sphere. A fragment of ZXW-calculus is interpreted projectively, yielding an alternate derivation of the arithmetic GHZ/W-calculus. Meromorphic functions characterize coherent behavior in circuits for logical state preparation of quantum codes and magic state distillation.
AI.motivation: To reformulate quantum mechanical kinematic axioms projectively, moving from normalized states up to global phase to one-dimensional subspaces, and to connect this projective formalism with diagrammatic calculi (ZXW-calculus, GHZ/W-calculus) for analyzing quantum circuits.
AI.method: The authors apply projectivization as a functorial, lax monoidal process that maps states to one-dimensional subspaces. For qubits, this identifies the Bloch sphere with the Riemann sphere. They interpret a fragment of the ZXW-calculus projectively to derive the arithmetic GHZ/W-calculus. Meromorphic functions are employed to characterize coherent behavior in circuits for logical state preparation and magic state distillation.
AI.result: An alternate derivation of the arithmetic GHZ/W-calculus is provided via projective interpretation of ZXW-calculus. Meromorphic functions are found that describe coherent behavior in circuits for logical state preparation of quantum codes and magic state distillation.
AI.conclusion: The projective formulation of quantum mechanics offers a clean mathematical framework (functorial, lax monoidal) that unifies the Bloch/Riemann sphere picture with diagrammatic quantum calculi, enabling new insights into quantum code preparation and magic state distillation.

title: Beating noise in frequency estimation with squeezing and memory in continuous-variable systems
summary: Quantum metrology promises precision beyond classical limits, yet environmental noise typically degrades the quantum resources required for such enhancement. In this work, we investigate frequency estimation in noisy continuous-variable systems, focusing on two complementary strategies to mitigate decoherence: Hamiltonian engineering and the exploitation of non-Markovian dynamics. By embedding squeezing directly into the system Hamiltonian, we show that the quantum Fisher information (QFI) may acquire a tunable higher-order time dependence, leading to enhanced sensitivity in the short-time regime. Moving beyond the Markovian approximation, we employ the quantum Brownian motion model to demonstrate that structured environments with finite memory can induce information backflow, temporarily restoring and even improving estimation precision relative to the unitary limit. We further assess the achievability of these bounds via Gaussian measurements, identifying regimes where homodyne, heterodyne, and optimized general-dyne measurements saturate the QFI, and noting that stronger squeezing widens the gap, potentially requiring non-Gaussian measurement strategies. Our results establish that jointly tailoring system Hamiltonian and environmental memory offers a viable route toward robust quantum-enhanced frequency estimation in open systems.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that frequency estimation in noisy continuous-variable systems can be enhanced by combining Hamiltonian engineering (embedding squeezing into the Hamiltonian) and exploiting non-Markovian dynamics (quantum Brownian motion with memory), achieving sensitivity beyond the unitary limit in the short-time regime, with Gaussian measurements approaching the QFI but stronger squeezing potentially requiring non-Gaussian strategies.
AI.motivation: Environmental noise degrades quantum resources needed for quantum metrology beyond classical limits; the authors aim to mitigate decoherence in frequency estimation for noisy continuous-variable systems.
AI.method: Two complementary strategies: (1) Hamiltonian engineering by embedding squeezing directly into the system Hamiltonian to introduce tunable higher-order time dependence in QFI; (2) exploiting non-Markovian dynamics via the quantum Brownian motion model with structured environments having finite memory to induce information backflow.
AI.result: Embedded squeezing yields enhanced short-time sensitivity; non-Markovian dynamics with memory can temporarily restore or even surpass the unitary limit. Homodyne, heterodyne, and optimized general-dyne measurements can saturate the QFI in certain regimes, but stronger squeezing widens the gap, potentially requiring non-Gaussian measurements.
AI.conclusion: Jointly tailoring the system Hamiltonian and environmental memory provides a viable route toward robust quantum-enhanced frequency estimation in open systems.

title: Local distillation from Reed Muller codes unfolding
summary: We generalize the unfolding of a Reed Muller distillation factory of Ruiz et. al. by exhibiting the algebraic structure that the unfolding is based on. We describe a 2D local layout for the Z stabilizers of a distance 4 Reed Muller distillation factory and a 3D local layout for the Z stabilizer of a distance 4 and a distance 7 Reed Muller distillation factory. Given input T states with infidelities $p=10^{-3}$, the 2D local distillation factory with distance 4 outputs a CCZ state with infidelity $p=8.256 \times 10^{-9}$ and the 3D local distillation factory with distance 7 outputs a T state with infidelity $p=1.1811 \times 10^{-17}$.

AI.tldr: This paper generalizes the unfolding of Reed-Muller distillation factories by revealing the underlying algebraic structure, and proposes 2D and 3D local layouts for Z stabilizers of distance 4 and distance 7 factories, achieving high-fidelity CCZ and T state outputs from noisy inputs.
AI.motivation: To generalize and improve the unfolding of Reed-Muller distillation factories by uncovering the algebraic structure that enables more efficient and higher-distance local layouts for magic state distillation.
AI.method: Algebraic generalization of Reed-Muller distillation factory unfolding; design of 2D local layout for Z stabilizers (distance 4) and 3D local layout (distance 4 and 7).
AI.result: With input T states at infidelity p=10^{-3}, the 2D distance-4 factory outputs a CCZ state at infidelity 8.256×10^{-9}; the 3D distance-7 factory outputs a T state at infidelity 1.1811×10^{-17}.
AI.conclusion: The algebraic structure of unfolding enables systematic construction of local layouts for Reed-Muller distillation factories, achieving significantly improved output fidelity at higher distances.

title: Macroscopic entanglement between two magnon modes via two-tone driving of a superconducting qubit
summary: The cavity-mediated coupling between magnons in an yttrium-iron-garnet (YIG) sphere and a superconducting qubit has recently been demonstrated as a new platform for preparing macroscopic quantum states. Here, based on this system, we propose to entangle two magnon modes in two YIG spheres by driving the qubit with a two-tone field and by appropriately choosing the frequencies and strengths of the two driving fields. We show that strong entanglement can be achieved with fully feasible parameters. We further provide a detection scheme for experimentally verifying the entanglement. Our results indicate that macroscopic entanglement between two magnon modes in two millimeter-sized YIG spheres, involving more than $10^{18}$ spins, can be realized using currently available parameters, which finds promising applications in fundamental studies, such as macroscopic quantum mechanics and the test of unconventional decoherence theories.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a scheme to entangle two magnon modes in two YIG spheres by driving a superconducting qubit with a two-tone field, achieving strong macroscopic entanglement (>10^18 spins) with experimentally feasible parameters.
AI.motivation: To develop a practical scheme for generating macroscopic entanglement between two magnon modes in two YIG spheres, building on recently demonstrated cavity-mediated coupling between magnons and superconducting qubits.
AI.method: The proposal uses a cavity-mediated coupling system where two YIG spheres are coupled to a superconducting qubit. The qubit is driven with a two-tone field, with carefully chosen frequencies and strengths, to entangle the two magnon modes.
AI.result: Strong entanglement between two magnon modes can be achieved with fully feasible parameters. A detection scheme for experimentally verifying the entanglement is also provided.
AI.conclusion: Macroscopic entanglement between two magnon modes in two millimeter-sized YIG spheres (involving >10^18 spins) can be realized with currently available parameters, with promising applications in macroscopic quantum mechanics and tests of unconventional decoherence theories.

title: Ablation Removal of Transport-Blocking Defects in Surface-Electrode Ion Traps
summary: We demonstrate in situ removal of a transport-blocking defect on a surface-electrode ion trap device using a Q-switched Nd:YAG 532 nm pulsed ablation laser. This approach eliminates the need to vent and rebake the vacuum system, providing a low-overhead defect-remediation technique well suited for ion-shuttling architectures where system modifications typically incur substantial downtime - particularly in shuttling focussed experiments operating at temperatures that necessitate bakes. Additionally, the hardware used is readily available in many ion trap laboratories, making this solution attractive to experiments operating in such regimes. Following ablation, we observe near-unit shuttling success rates across the previously obstructed region and measure micromotion levels that remain within acceptable limits. This technique enables rapid, reliable restoration of transport pathways without interruption to experimental operation.

AI.tldr: A Q-switched Nd:YAG 532 nm pulsed ablation laser is used to remove a transport-blocking defect on a surface-electrode ion trap in situ, avoiding vacuum system venting and rebaking, and restoring near-unit shuttling success with acceptable micromotion.
AI.motivation: Defects in ion trap transport pathways typically require venting and rebaking the vacuum system, causing substantial downtime—especially for shuttling-focused experiments that operate at temperatures necessitating bakes. A low-overhead, in situ remediation technique is needed.
AI.method: A Q-switched Nd:YAG 532 nm pulsed ablation laser was used to ablate a transport-blocking defect on a surface-electrode ion trap under vacuum, without venting or rebaking.
AI.result: Near-unit shuttling success rates were achieved across the previously obstructed region, and micromotion levels remained within acceptable limits.
AI.conclusion: Pulsed ablation laser cleaning enables rapid, reliable restoration of ion transport pathways without interrupting experimental operation, using hardware already common in ion trap laboratories.

title: Coherence limitations of a Fourier-engineered $\cos(2\varphi)$ transmon qubit
summary: Intrinsically protected superconducting qubits are a promising route toward enhancing coherence times and advancing hardware towards applications in quantum computing. The $\cos(2\varphi)$ qubit achieves protection against qubit relaxation by allowing only the coherent tunneling of pairs of Cooper pairs, resulting in Cooper-pair parity symmetry and thereby suppressing charge-induced errors. In this work, we experimentally realize a $\cos(2\varphi)$ qubit by Fourier engineering the energy-phase relation in a multi-junction superconducting circuit. Using an interference-based architecture, we are able to suppress the odd harmonics of an effective qubit potential and we observe good agreement between the measured transition spectrum and the effective theoretical model. We further investigate the energy relaxation time as a function of external flux and find that the qubit lifetime at the flux symmetry point is limited by $1/f$ flux noise. This strong sensitivity arises from residual fluctuations in the first harmonic, which possesses a large prefactor despite being nominally canceled. In contrast, a fluxonium qubit with a similar energy spectrum and noise amplitude is less affected by flux noise, highlighting a key challenge for interference-based protection schemes.

AI.tldr: The paper experimentally realizes a $\cos(2\varphi)$ qubit using a multi-junction interference-based architecture that suppresses odd harmonics to achieve Cooper-pair parity symmetry. The qubit shows good agreement with theory but its lifetime is limited by $1/f$ flux noise due to residual first harmonic fluctuations, and it is more sensitive to flux noise than a comparable fluxonium qubit.
AI.motivation: To experimentally realize a $\cos(2\varphi)$ qubit that achieves intrinsic protection against qubit relaxation via Cooper-pair parity symmetry, thereby suppressing charge-induced errors and enhancing coherence times for quantum computing applications.
AI.method: Fourier engineering the energy-phase relation in a multi-junction superconducting circuit using an interference-based architecture to suppress odd harmonics of the effective qubit potential.
AI.result: Good agreement between measured transition spectrum and theoretical model; qubit lifetime at the flux symmetry point is limited by $1/f$ flux noise due to residual first harmonic fluctuations with a large prefactor, making it more sensitive to flux noise than a fluxonium qubit with similar energy spectrum.
AI.conclusion: While the $\cos(2\varphi)$ qubit is realized and shows protection against charge noise, its interference-based protection scheme is vulnerable to flux noise from residual first harmonic content, highlighting a key challenge for such architectures compared to alternative designs like fluxonium.

title: Photonic-Implemented Efficient Deep Quantum Neural Network via Virtual-Driven Hilbert Space Expansion
summary: The growing computational demands of classical neural networks have intensified the search for energy-efficient and powerful computational alternatives. Quantum neural networks (QNNs) implemented on integrated photonic platforms offer a compelling avenue, offering exceptional computational power enhancements, with inherent programmability and scalability of integrated architectures. A critical challenge, however, is implementing the fundamental non-unitary and nonlinear activation function of QNNs within a linear quantum photonic system. Existing strategies, such as the adding ancillary qubits and measurement-based feedback or forward are constrained by high qubit resource costs, overhead devices, and poor cascadability. Here, we propose a novel deep photonic QNN with an expanded computational Hilbert space via input replication and mode expansion, which enables the realization of effective non-unitary and nonlinear activation on a linear programmable quantum photonic chip. This approach eliminates the need for physical ancillary qubits, measurement-induced qubit consumption and the measurement device burden, thereby significantly reduce resource costs. The fabricated chip integrates four high-quality entanglement sources and a programmable high-dimensional interferometric network, enabling a two-hidden-layer QNN that exhibits dimension-enhanced expressivity over the existing QNN architectures. We demonstrate its capabilities across diverse tasks, including nonlinear classification, image generation, and quantum Gibbs state preparation. This work establishes a scalable and efficient architecture toward practical quantum deep learning systems capable of tackling problems beyond the reach of classical computation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a deep photonic quantum neural network that achieves non-unitary and nonlinear activation functions on a linear programmable quantum photonic chip via input replication and mode expansion, eliminating the need for physical ancillary qubits and measurement devices, and demonstrates enhanced expressivity across classification, image generation, and quantum state preparation tasks.
AI.motivation: To address the high resource costs and poor cascadability of existing methods for implementing non-unitary and nonlinear activation functions in quantum neural networks on integrated photonic platforms.
AI.method: A deep photonic QNN architecture using input replication and mode expansion to expand the computational Hilbert space, enabling effective non-unitary and nonlinear activation on a linear programmable quantum photonic chip without physical ancillary qubits or measurement-induced qubit consumption.
AI.result: A fabricated chip integrating four high-quality entanglement sources and a programmable high-dimensional interferometric network, realizing a two-hidden-layer QNN with dimension-enhanced expressivity, demonstrated on nonlinear classification, image generation, and quantum Gibbs state preparation.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes a scalable and efficient architecture for practical quantum deep learning systems capable of tackling problems beyond classical computational reach.
