title: Multitime memory beyond the quantum regression theorem in sequential measurement statistics
summary: We investigate the presence of memory in the sequential measurement statistics of an open quantum system, as witnessed by the departure from the quantum regression theorem (QRT), that is, the possibility to predict multitime probabilities from the one-time reduced dynamical map. For factorized initial states, we identify an exact decomposition of the two-time propagator into a QRT-like contribution, fully determined by the reduced dynamical map, and a memory term encoding system--environment correlations across the intervention; in the weak-coupling regime, the memory term yields an explicit second-order correction expressed in terms of the reduced map and bath correlation functions. Furthermore, we introduce an operational quantifier of QRT violations based on the distance between exact and QRT-predicted joint probabilities. Benchmarking the framework on a spin--boson model and using a pseudomode embedding as nonperturbative reference, we comprehensively analyze the impact of spectral-density parameters, environmental temperature, and measurement protocols on the non-Markovianity of the multitime statistics. Comparison with a one-time quantifier shows that reduced-state non-Markovianity and multitime memory are related but inequivalent: the latter, as probed through sequential statistics, is intrinsically protocol dependent and can become visible at higher temporal order even when two-time statistics remain compatible with QRT predictions.

AI.tldr: This paper examines violations of the quantum regression theorem (QRT) in open quantum systems, deriving an exact decomposition of two-time propagators into QRT and memory terms, computing weak-coupling corrections, and introducing an operational quantifier for QRT violations. Using a spin-boson model with pseudomode embedding, they show that multitime memory is protocol-dependent and can appear even when reduced-state dynamics appear Markovian.
AI.motivation: To understand memory effects in sequential measurement statistics of open quantum systems by analyzing departures from the quantum regression theorem, which assumes multitime probabilities can be predicted from the one-time reduced dynamical map.
AI.method: (1) Derivation of an exact decomposition of the two-time propagator into a QRT-like contribution and a memory term encoding system-environment correlations. (2) Second-order weak-coupling correction expressed via reduced map and bath correlation functions. (3) Introduction of an operational quantifier based on distance between exact and QRT-predicted joint probabilities. (4) Numerical benchmarking on a spin-boson model using pseudomode embedding as nonperturbative reference.
AI.result: (1) Exact decomposition of two-time propagator valid for factorized initial states. (2) Explicit second-order memory correction in weak coupling. (3) Reduced-state non-Markovianity and multitime memory are inequivalent—multitime memory is protocol-dependent and can appear at higher temporal orders even when two-time statistics follow QRT. (4) Systematic analysis of spectral-density parameters, temperature, and measurement protocols on multitime non-Markovianity.
AI.conclusion: Multitime memory effects in open quantum systems are fundamentally distinct from reduced-state non-Markovianity, requiring direct probing of sequential statistics. The QRT violation quantifier provides a protocol-dependent measure that captures memory invisible to one-time quantifiers.

title: Revisiting the multi-mode rhombus circuit as a biased-noise qubit
summary: In this work, we revisit the idea of using an interferometer of pairs of Josephson junctions as a protected rhombus qubit. Unlike in the original proposal, where the qubit states are encoded into odd and even parity charge states, here, we intentionally alter the energy of one of the junctions to investigate the soft version of the rhombus qubit. This approach allows us to directly probe the qubit transitions over several GHz and reduce the potential drawbacks of the interferometer-based protection. Away from a half flux quantum external field, the large shunting capacitors of the circuit ensure localized qubit states in different phase valleys, leading to a biased-noise qubit. In the realized circuit, we measure an average $T_1\approx500\,μ$s relaxation time in the biased-noise regime (with a Ramsey dephasing time of $T^{R}_\varphi\approx90\,$ns), while an average $T_1\approx27\,μ$s relaxation time at frustration (with $T^{R}_\varphi\approx670\,$ns). Our loss analysis on this multi-mode circuit indicates that at low frequencies, flux noise and quasiparticle tunneling limit the relaxation times, pointing toward the presence of an optimal operating regime of around a few GHz.

AI.tldr: The paper experimentally revisits the protected rhombus qubit using an interferometer of Josephson junction pairs, introducing an intentionally altered junction energy to create a "soft" version. This enables direct probing of qubit transitions in the GHz range. The circuit exhibits biased-noise properties away from half-flux quantum, achieving T₁ ≈ 500 μs (biased-noise) vs T₁ ≈ 27 μs (at frustration), with flux noise and quasiparticle tunneling as dominant loss mechanisms at low frequencies.
AI.motivation: To revisit and improve the original protected rhombus qubit design by introducing a "soft" version that allows direct GHz-range probing of qubit transitions while mitigating drawbacks of interferometer-based protection.
AI.method: The authors modify one junction's energy in a pair of Josephson junction interferometers to create a soft rhombus qubit, use large shunting capacitors for phase valley localization away from half-flux quantum, and perform experimental characterization of relaxation and dephasing times in both biased-noise and frustrated regimes.
AI.result: Average T₁ ≈ 500 μs (Ramsey dephasing T_φ^R ≈ 90 ns) in biased-noise regime; average T₁ ≈ 27 μs (T_φ^R ≈ 670 ns) at frustration. Loss analysis identifies flux noise and quasiparticle tunneling as limiting relaxation at low frequencies, with optimal operation around a few GHz.
AI.conclusion: The soft rhombus qubit design enables direct probing of transitions at GHz frequencies while maintaining biased-noise protection away from frustration. An optimal operating regime exists around a few GHz where performance is maximized, balancing the trade-off between relaxation and dephasing times.

title: Tight Contraction Rates for Primitive Channels under Quantum $f$-Divergences
summary: Data-processing inequalities capture the phenomenon that two probability distributions can only become less distinguishable under any common post-processing. For more fine-grained inequalities, one turns to strong data-processing inequality (SDPI) constants, which give the strongest inequalities for a given channel and reference state for a fixed measure of distinguishability. These quantities have been used to quantify the rate at which time-homogeneous Markov chains contract towards a fixed point both in the classical and quantum setting. In this work, we establish that quantum $f$-divergences satisfy a local reverse Pinsker inequality, which implies the asymptotic contraction rate of a primitive channel to its stationary state is upper bounded by the SDPI constant of any non-commutative $χ^2$-divergence. Using quantum-detailed balance, we establish a sufficient condition for these bounds to be tight. Finally, we apply these results to Petz, Matsumoto, and Hirche-Tomamichel $f$-divergences, establishing new and strengthening previously known results.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes that quantum f-divergences satisfy a local reverse Pinsker inequality, linking asymptotic contraction rates of primitive quantum channels to SDPI constants of non-commutative χ²-divergences, with tightness conditions via quantum-detailed balance.
AI.motivation: To provide finer-grained data-processing inequalities in quantum information theory by connecting SDPI constants of quantum f-divergences to asymptotic contraction rates of primitive quantum channels.
AI.method: Establishes a local reverse Pinsker inequality for quantum f-divergences; relates asymptotic contraction rates to SDPI constants of non-commutative χ²-divergences; uses quantum-detailed balance to derive tightness conditions.
AI.result: Asymptotic contraction rate of a primitive channel to its stationary state is upper bounded by the SDPI constant of any non-commutative χ²-divergence; sufficient condition for tightness via quantum-detailed balance; new and strengthened results for Petz, Matsumoto, and Hirche-Tomamichel divergences.
AI.conclusion: Quantum f-divergences admit a local reverse Pinsker inequality, enabling tighter contraction rate bounds for quantum Markov chains, with applications to specific divergence families.

title: Entanglement generation in a two-body Schrödinger--Newton model
summary: The Schrödinger--Newton (SN) equation provides a semiclassical framework for the evolution of self-gravitating of massive quantum systems. We propose a two-body Schrödinger--Newton model that separates local nonlinear self-localization from the nonseparable Newtonian pair potential. Analytically, we show that the nonlinear self-field preserves the Schmidt spectrum, whereas direct entanglement generation arises from the nonseparable pair potential. Using numerical simulations in a regularized one-dimensional geometry, we find that entanglement generation depends sensitively on the initial spatial configuration and on the mass ratio. Highly localized, self-bound wavepackets experience minimal entanglement growth during scattering. Spatial delocalization and kinetic dispersion broaden the interaction region, amplifying the entangling power of the pair potential and exciting higher-order spatial modes. For dispersive Gaussian initial states, mass asymmetry shatters the lighter particle, producing Wigner negativity and rapid entanglement growth, whereas stationary SN profiles strongly suppress this effect. Stationary SN profiles isolate the bare pair-potential contribution; dispersive Gaussian initial states inflate it.

AI.tldr: This paper studies a two-body Schrödinger-Newton model, showing that nonlinear self-localization preserves the Schmidt spectrum while the nonseparable pair potential generates entanglement. Entanglement depends sensitively on initial spatial configuration and mass ratio; stationary SN profiles suppress entanglement, while dispersive Gaussian states amplify it.
AI.motivation: To understand how semiclassical gravity (via the SN equation) affects entanglement dynamics in massive quantum systems, particularly separating the roles of nonlinear self-localization versus the Newtonian pair potential.
AI.method: Analytical derivation showing the nonlinear self-field preserves the Schmidt spectrum, combined with numerical simulations in a regularized one-dimensional geometry to study entanglement generation under various initial conditions and mass ratios.
AI.result: Entanglement generation depends sensitively on initial spatial configuration and mass ratio. Localized self-bound wavepackets show minimal entanglement growth; dispersive Gaussian states amplify it. Mass asymmetry shatters the lighter particle, producing Wigner negativity and rapid entanglement growth. Stationary SN profiles suppress these effects.
AI.conclusion: The nonlinear self-field does not generate entanglement (preserves Schmidt spectrum); only the nonseparable Newtonian pair potential does. Stationary SN profiles isolate bare pair-potential entanglement, while dispersive initial states inflate it, suggesting careful initial state preparation is crucial for observing semiclassical gravity effects on entanglement.

title: Practical Log-Depth Quantum State Preparation and Circuit Verification via Tree Tensor Network Compilation
summary: Matrix product states provide efficient classical descriptions of quantum systems that may be useful as reference states for quantum algorithms such as quantum phase estimation and quantum-selected configuration interaction. Shallow circuit constructions for loading matrix product states onto quantum computers is necessary for this to be practical on near-term hardware. We present a decomposition of matrix product states to log-depth quantum circuits via a simple tree tensor network renormalisation procedure. Our method exposes an explicit parameter which can be used to trade a small amount of fidelity for large savings in circuit depth. We extend this decomposition to the case of matrix product operators allowing us to construct log-depth and ancilla-free circuits to calculate overlaps of the form $\left |\langleφ|U|ψ\rangle\right |^2$. In particular, we demonstrate an interpretation of these circuits as \emph{verifier circuits} with application to circuit-level device calibration.

AI.tldr: Matrix product states can be decomposed into log-depth quantum circuits via tree tensor network renormalization, enabling efficient quantum state preparation with tunable fidelity-depth tradeoffs and verifier circuits for calibration.
AI.motivation: Matrix product states (MPS) are useful reference states for quantum algorithms like quantum phase estimation and selected configuration interaction, but loading them onto quantum computers with shallow circuits is necessary for near-term hardware practicality.
AI.method: The authors present a decomposition of MPS into log-depth quantum circuits using a tree tensor network renormalization procedure. The method exposes a tunable parameter for fidelity-depth tradeoffs and extends to matrix product operators for constructing ancilla-free circuits to compute overlaps.
AI.result: Log-depth quantum circuits for loading MPS and MPOs are achieved; circuits for computing overlaps of the form |⟨φ|U|ψ⟩|² are constructed without ancilla qubits.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables practical MPS state preparation on near-term quantum hardware with shallow circuits, and the overlap circuits can serve as verifier circuits for device-level calibration.

title: Machine Learning Approaches to Building Quantum Circuits for Sets of Matrices
summary: Machine learning nowadays becomes a useful instrument in many subjects. In this paper we use interpretable machine learning to build quantum algorithm. By studying the parameters of the machine learning algorithm we were able to construct universal shortest analytic quantum algorithm for arbitrary diagonal matrix of any size.

AI.tldr: This paper uses interpretable machine learning to construct a universal shortest analytic quantum algorithm for arbitrary diagonal matrices of any size.
AI.motivation: To leverage interpretable machine learning as a tool for designing quantum algorithms, specifically targeting the problem of constructing efficient quantum algorithms for diagonal matrices.
AI.method: The authors apply interpretable machine learning techniques and analyze the parameters of the learned model to derive a universal shortest analytic quantum algorithm for arbitrary diagonal matrices of any size.
AI.result: A universal shortest analytic quantum algorithm for arbitrary diagonal matrices of any size was successfully constructed.
AI.conclusion: Interpretable machine learning can serve as a useful instrument for systematically constructing quantum algorithms, demonstrated by the derivation of a shortest analytic algorithm for diagonal matrices.
